skill.name: Predict from clues, then check
skill.why: Good readers guess what's coming, then read on to see if they were right.
skill.how: Spot the clues, ask what they point to, make a guess, then check it.

steps.say: Stories drop clues before something big happens. I keep my eyes open.

show.nudge: Tuesday is just the day. What strange thing happens?
A cold pie is sad, but it doesn't warn you of anything.

steps.ask: Tap the clue that something big is coming.
steps.win: Yes! Shaking ground is a clue. Thump, thump... something is on its way.

steps.say: Then a huge shadow falls over Zed. That's me! What do the clues point to?

show.text: A huge shadow fell over Zed.

options.text: Something giant will stomp into view.
A tiny mouse will run past.
options.reason: A tiny mouse can't shake the ground or make a huge shadow.

options.text: It will start to snow.
options.reason: Snow doesn't go thump. No clue points to snow.

steps.win: Yes! A guess that the clues back up is called a prediction.

steps.say: Mo has a guess too. He's hungry, so he yells, 'It's the pizza delivery!'

show.text: A huge shadow fell over Zed.

steps.ask: Which guess is a wish, not a prediction?

options.text: A pizza is coming, because Mo is hungry.
Something giant is coming.
options.reason: Shaking ground and a huge shadow back this up. It's a prediction.

options.text: A huge truck is coming.
options.reason: A truck could shake the ground. The clues back this up.

steps.win: Yes! No clue points to pizza. Mo just wants one. That's a wish, not a prediction.

steps.say: Now I read on to check my prediction.

show.nudge: That's my prediction. Read on. Which part shows if I was right?
Looking up doesn't tell you what's there. Read on.

show.text: A giant robot stomped round the corner.

show.nudge: Poor pie! But what came round the corner?

steps.ask: Tap the part that checks my prediction.
steps.win: Yes! A giant robot. My prediction was right. Good readers always read on to check.

steps.say: Sometimes the check shows I was wrong. Then I change my prediction.

show.text: Then the wind blew the clouds away, and the sun came out.

steps.ask: I predicted rain. What should I do now?

options.text: Change it. Rain is less likely now.
Keep it. Clouds always mean rain.
options.reason: Read the last part again. Where did the clouds go?

options.text: Stop reading. I already made my guess.
options.reason: Good readers keep reading and checking. New clues can change things.

steps.win: Yes! New clues can change a prediction. Check, then change it if you need to.

steps.say: Tully predicts the Reef Rays will win on Saturday. Some details help predict. Some don't.

show.nudge: Ten wins in a row makes a win more likely. That helps.

show.text: Their best player hurt her knee.
show.nudge: A hurt player makes a win less likely. That still helps.

steps.ask: Tap the detail that doesn't help predict who wins.
steps.win: Yes! New socks won't change the score. Think about every clue, and skip the ones that don't matter.

terms.means: A detail that hints at what might happen next.
Your best guess about what comes next, backed up by clues.
Read on. Were you right? If not, change your prediction.

examples.text: The dog stared at Mo's pie.
The dog will grab the pie.

card.test: Spot the clues. Guess where they point. Read on and check. A wish is not a prediction.

weDo.success: Two hours and black smoke are the clues. Mo opened the oven. The cake was a lump of charcoal.

options.text: a burnt cake

weDo.prompt: Which prediction do the clues support best?
weDo.hint: What do dark clouds and umbrellas usually mean?
weDo.success: Clouds, umbrellas and wind all point to rain. Two minutes later, the oval was a swamp.

creature.name: Hintatoo
creature.blurb: A sulphur-crested cockatoo that keeps lookout for its flock. It reads the clues, screeches what's coming, then waits to see if it was right.

encounters.frame: A page from Mo's diary is stuck in the Hintatoo's tree.
encounters.text: Last night I heard a scratching sound in the kitchen. Scratch, scratch, scratch. I crept down the stairs with a torch. The biscuit tin was on the floor. Its lid was off. There was a trail of crumbs across the tiles. The crumbs led to a small hole in the wall. Two tiny eyes were shining in the hole. Then I heard a squeak.
encounters.prompt: What will Mo find when he shines his torch into the hole?
encounters.success: Tiny eyes, a squeak and crumbs leading to a hole. A fat mouse was munching a choc-chip biscuit.

options.text: a mouse eating biscuits
a ghost
options.reason: Ghosts don't leave crumbs or squeak. Tiny eyes in a small hole point to a small animal.

options.text: a lost dog
options.reason: A dog couldn't fit in a small hole, and its eyes wouldn't be tiny.

encounters.frame: Tully is commentating sports day on the school speaker.
encounters.text: It was sports day, and Mia was in the 100 metre race. She was out in front. But her shoelace had come undone. It flapped with every step. 'I predict Mia will trip on that lace,' Tully said into the microphone. The finish line was just ahead. Then Mia's foot came down right on the lace. She tripped and rolled over and over. She rolled across the finish line! Mia came second.
encounters.prompt: Tully predicted Mia would trip. Read on. What does the check show?
encounters.success: The check agrees. Mia's foot came down on the lace and she tripped, so Tully was right.

options.text: Tully was wrong. Mia won the race easily.
options.reason: Read the end. Mia came second, and she rolled over the line.

options.text: Tully was right. Mia tripped over her lace.
Tully was wrong. Mia stopped to tie her lace.
options.reason: Mia never stops. Her foot comes down on the lace. What happens then?

encounters.frame: Wren's snorkelling diary is soggy, but you can still read it.
encounters.text: Day 3 at Seal Rock. Indi and I snorkelled from our boat to the old shipwreck. Before we got in, the skipper gave us one rule. If anything big comes near, swim straight back to the boat. Hundreds of tiny silver fish swam around us. Then every single fish darted into the wreck and hid. A big grey shadow slid across the sand below us. I predicted a shark, so we raced back to the boat. We climbed up the ladder, puffing hard. Then a whiskery face popped out of the water beside us. It rolled over, blew bubbles and waited for a pat. 'That's Sid, our seal,' laughed the skipper. 'He's a big softie.'
encounters.prompt: Wren predicted the shadow was a shark. Read on. What does the check show?
encounters.success: The check changes it. The shadow was Sid the seal. Swimming back was still the skipper's rule, so well done.

options.text: She was right. It was something big and dangerous.
options.reason: It was big. But it blows bubbles and waits for a pat. Is that dangerous?

options.text: She was wrong. The shadow was a friendly seal.

encounters.frame: Zed is going for a speedrun record. The Hintatoo is watching over his shoulder.
encounters.text: Zed was one level away from the fastest time ever. His hands were sweaty. His thumbs ached. The timer said 59 minutes and 40 seconds. He needed to beat the boss in under twenty seconds. The boss was a giant slime that split in two whenever you hit it. It wobbled and growled. Zed had a secret plan. Instead of hitting the slime, he jumped right over it. There was a lever on the wall that nobody ever used. Zed had read about it on an old game forum. The lever held up a huge iron cage, which hung right above the slime.
encounters.prompt: Which prediction do the clues support best?
encounters.success: The lever holds a cage right above the slime. CLANG! The cage dropped, and Zed finished in 59:58.

options.text: Zed pulls the lever and traps the slime.
Zed hits the slime as hard as he can.
options.reason: Hitting the slime makes it split in two. Zed's plan is to stop hitting it.

options.text: Zed gives up and switches off the game.
options.reason: Zed has a secret plan and is one level from a record. Nothing hints that he'll quit.

encounters.frame: Tully is exploring the old clock tower. The Hintatoo refuses to go in.
encounters.text: The old clock tower had been empty for fifty years. At least, that's what the sign said. Tully pushed the heavy door open. It creaked. Her torch flickered. Cobwebs hung from the ceiling like old curtains, and the wind howled outside. Grey feathers were scattered across the bottom step. A mouse skeleton lay in the corner, picked perfectly clean. White splats ran all the way up the stairs, and they smelled terrible. Tully heard a soft hoot from the top of the tower. Then came a flap and a rustle. Something up there was shaking out its wings. She took a deep breath and started to climb.
encounters.prompt: What will Tully find at the top of the stairs?
encounters.success: Feathers, splats, a hoot and flapping wings. At the top, a huge owl blinked at Tully from its nest.

options.text: a big bird nesting at the top
a caretaker who still lives there
options.reason: People don't hoot or shake out wings. The feathers and splats point to a bird.

options.text: nothing, because the tower is empty
options.reason: The hoot and the flapping show that something is up there right now.

encounters.frame: Indi is backstage at the school concert, scribbling notes.
encounters.text: The Year 6 band had practised every lunchtime for a month. Tonight was the big concert, and the hall was packed. Indi peeked out from backstage. The lights over the stage kept flickering on and off. The microphone squealed every time someone touched it. Ava, the singer, had a sore throat and could only croak. But the trumpet players knew every note by heart. They were warming up quietly in the corner, grinning. Mr Lee gave everyone a thumbs up. "Two minutes!" he called. Some little kids in the front row were already clapping. Indi crossed her fingers and wrote down what she had seen.

encounters.success: Clues can point different ways. The lights did go out, but the trumpets played on in the dark.

encounters.text: Dear crew, I have made a surprise dinner! It is in the big pot on the stove. I used every leftover in the fridge. Gus tasted it and ran straight to the sink. He drank four glasses of water. Then he went a funny shade of green. Tully took one sniff and opened all the windows. I think they just love it! Come and get it! Love, Mo

encounters.frame: Tully is reading the sports page of the Hollowgum Herald out loud.
encounters.text:
DRAMA AT THE POOL

Nobody expected much from twelve-year-old Pia Moretti in last night's 200 metre freestyle final. At the halfway mark, she was dead last, a full body length behind the leader. Most of the crowd had stopped watching her. But her coach, sitting by the pool, didn't look worried at all. In fact, he was smiling. Pia had swum the same way in every race this season. She always swims the first half slowly to save her energy for the end. Her rivals, meanwhile, had gone out as fast as they could. By the third lap, the leader's arms were slapping the water, and her head was bobbing up and down. The swimmer in second place kept grabbing at the lane rope. Pia's stroke looked exactly the same as it had at the start: long, smooth and steady. With one lap to go, she took a deep breath and put her head down.
encounters.prompt: What will most likely happen in the last lap?
encounters.success: She saved her energy while her rivals tired. Pia flew past every swimmer and touched the wall first.

options.text: Pia speeds up and passes the tired swimmers.
Pia stays last because she is too far behind.
options.reason: She's only one body length back, and she's been saving energy for this. Her coach is smiling.

options.text: The leader speeds up and wins easily.
options.reason: The leader's arms are slapping and her head is bobbing. She's tiring, not speeding up.

options.text: Pia runs out of energy and slows down.
options.reason: Pia's stroke is still smooth and steady. She saved her energy, so she isn't the tired one.

encounters.frame: Gus has built a cleaning robot. The Hintatoo has raised its crest.
encounters.text: Gus had finally finished his cleaning robot, Sweepy. Its job was simple: find anything sticky, smelly or slimy, and get rid of it. On its first morning, Sweepy did brilliantly. It binned a mouldy apple core from under the couch. It binned a pair of Mo's socks that could stand up on their own. It even binned a melted lolly that had been glued to the carpet since Easter. Gus was thrilled. "Sweepy never stops until a job is done," he told the crew. "Not even if you beg." Then he grinned. "Now," he said proudly, "come and see my real masterpiece." He opened the lab door. On the bench sat his prize project: Slimeon, a giant bucket of glowing green slime that had taken him six months to grow. It was sticky. It was smelly. It was very, very slimy. Sweepy's eye turned red. Its arms reached forward. Gus was too busy showing off to notice.
encounters.prompt: Which prediction do the clues support best?
encounters.success: Slimeon is sticky, smelly and slimy: Sweepy's whole job. SPLOOSH. Into the wheelie bin it went.

options.text: Sweepy will put Slimeon straight in the bin.
Sweepy will clean the lab floor around the bucket.
options.reason: Sweepy bins anything sticky, smelly or slimy. Slimeon is all three, so it won't be left alone.

options.text: Sweepy will leave Slimeon alone, because Gus loves it.
options.reason: That's what Gus would wish. No clue says Sweepy cares what Gus loves. Check Sweepy's job.

options.text: Gus will switch Sweepy off just in time.
options.reason: The text says Gus is too busy showing off to notice. He won't see it coming.

encounters.frame: The crew picked up a log from a space station passing over Hollowgum Island.
encounters.text:
Captain's log, Space Station Kestrel, Day 41.

Something strange is happening on board. Every night this week, a packet of dried strawberries has gone missing from the food locker. The locker has a keypad, and apart from me, only three crew know the code. Commander Ruiz hates strawberries. She says they taste like sweet cardboard, and she always swaps hers for crackers. Dr Okafor has been outside on a spacewalk every night this week, fixing the solar panels, so he hasn't been inside after dinner at all. Engineer Bao says he has been fast asleep in his sleeping pod. But yesterday I noticed tiny pink crumbs floating around the door of Bao's pod. This morning, his fingertips were stained red. When I mentioned the missing strawberries at breakfast, he suddenly remembered he had to check the engines, and floated off very fast. Tonight, I'm going to hide behind the food locker and watch.
encounters.prompt: Who will the captain most likely catch at the locker tonight?
encounters.success: Pink crumbs, red fingers, a sudden escape. At midnight, Bao floated up to the locker, licking his lips.

options.text: Engineer Bao
Commander Ruiz
options.reason: Ruiz hates strawberries and swaps hers for crackers. She has no reason to take them.

options.text: Dr Okafor
options.reason: Okafor is outside on a spacewalk every night, so he can't be at the locker.

options.text: Nobody, because the packets are floating away
options.reason: The locker is locked with a keypad, so packets can't drift out. Someone who knows the code is taking them.

encounters.text: The Hollowgum mural contest ends at noon, and it is already half past eleven. Indi has painted a huge orange sunset with pink clouds, but the whole top of the wall is still bare. She hasn't even started on the sky. This year the judges have asked for bright, bold colours, and Indi's mural glows. Out over the sea, dark clouds are rolling in, and the paint on her wall is still wet. Indi's brushes are getting stiff, so she keeps stopping to wash them. The crew are sitting on the grass with a bag of hot chips. Gus has known Indi since kindergarten, and he cheers every time she picks up a brush. Mo wants to eat his lunch outside on the oval. Everyone has a prediction, and Zed writes each one down in his notebook.

encounters.frame: Mo is running the sausage sizzle at the school fete. Zed's prediction has a word that doesn't fit.
encounters.text: The school fete started at nine, and Mo was in charge of the sausage sizzle. He had bought two hundred sausages, which he was very proud of. Unfortunately, he had also forgotten the bread. Tully raced home to fetch some, but her house is forty minutes away by bike. Meanwhile, a long line of hungry families had formed in front of the barbecue. Mo cooked the first fifty sausages anyway and piled them on a tray behind him. Within minutes, the smell had drifted across the whole oval. Then a seagull landed on the edge of the barbecue. Then another landed. Then about thirty more arrived. The seagulls stood perfectly still, staring at the tray with their beady eyes. One of them hopped a little closer. The families in the line started to grumble. Mo was busy waving his tongs at the line, shouting, "Bread's coming, I promise!" He did not look behind him at the tray of cooked sausages.

encounters.frame: A story is going round the campfire on Hollowgum Island. The Hintatoo's crest is standing straight up.
encounters.text: Camp Ironbark, night three. The campfire had burned down to a sullen orange glow when Hamish first saw the light. It hovered above the lake, pale and wobbling, about a hundred metres from shore. "That's her," whispered Priya, gripping her marshmallow stick. "The Lady of the Lake. Mr Okoro told us about her on the first night. She drifts across the water, searching for campers who haven't brushed their teeth." Nobody laughed. The light crept slowly towards the jetty. As it came closer, a steady splash, splash, splash carried across the water, as regular as a ticking clock. Hamish glanced around the circle of faces. Everyone from Cabin 4 was there. The camp cook was snoring in her deckchair. But Mr Okoro's chair, the one with the squeaky leg, was empty, and his marshmallows sat untouched beside it. Earlier that afternoon, Hamish had noticed that one of the camp kayaks was missing from the rack. He had also seen Mr Okoro carrying a white bedsheet and a head torch towards the boatshed, humming to himself and grinning in a way that made Hamish deeply suspicious. The light reached the end of the jetty and stopped. A low, wobbly voice moaned, "Whooo hasn't brushed their teeeeeth?" Hamish reached for the big spotlight and switched it on.

encounters.frame: Maxx Vantablack is live again, and this time he's after a Hintatoo.
encounters.text: What's up, Vantafam! It's your boy Maxx Vantablack, coming to you live from the deepest, darkest gully on Hollowgum Island. Tonight I'm finally going to "rescue" a wild Hintatoo. These birds are super rare, and everybody says they're impossible to catch, because they sit completely still for hours, studying everything around them before they move a single feather. But nobody is smarter than Maxx. Last week three of my traps failed, but that was totally Jono's fault. Check out my genius trap. I've tipped a pile of sunflower seeds on this rock, right under my net. When the Hintatoo swoops down for the seeds, my assistant Jono pulls the rope, and BAM, the net drops. Simple. This one's going straight into my private collection. I mean, the rescue centre. Okay, Jono, get ready. Jono? Why are you sneezing? Oh, great, he's allergic to feathers. Anyway, the Hintatoo is right there on that branch, staring at us. It's been staring for twenty minutes. It's blinking really slowly, which is kind of creepy. It's looked at the seeds, then at the net, then at the rope, then at Jono, then back at the net. Honestly, it's almost like it's thinking. Whatever, it's just a bird. Here it comes, Vantafam! It's spreading its wings! It's leaning towards the seeds...
encounters.prompt: Why does the writer show the Hintatoo looking at the seeds, the net, the rope and Jono?
encounters.success: The writer plants clues so you can predict it. The bird grabbed the seeds; the net fell on Maxx.

options.text: to show the reader that the bird is hungry for the seeds
options.reason: It looks at the net and the rope too. A hungry bird would only look at the seeds.

options.text: to show that Maxx's trap is clever enough to work
options.reason: Maxx thinks so. But a bird that studies every part of the trap is hard to fool.

options.text: to drop clues that the bird has worked out the trap
to make the stream feel slow and boring for the Vantafam
options.reason: The slow looking makes you lean in, not yawn. What is the bird checking, one thing at a time?

encounters.frame: Tully circled this story in the Hollowgum Herald and wrote her prediction in the margin.
encounters.text:
SANDCASTLE CHAMPIONSHIP GOES AHEAD DESPITE WARNINGS

Organisers of the Hollowgum Sandcastle Championship have refused to move tomorrow's event, even though the weather service has issued a king tide warning for the entire coast. The championship begins at 1 pm on the flat stretch of sand below Gull Point, where competitors will have exactly three hours to build. More than sixty teams are expected, and the castles will be judged at the end of the three hours. According to the tide chart pinned up at the surf club, high tide will arrive at 3:40 pm, and it is expected to be the highest tide of the year. Locals say that even during an ordinary high tide, the water reaches the bottom of the Gull Point stairs, and Gull Point is the lowest part of the beach. Some families have asked for the start to be moved to the morning, when the tide is out. Last year's champion, eleven-year-old Archie Tran, said he wasn't worried. "I'm building a moat this year," he said. "A really deep one." Head organiser Bev Saddler insists the event is perfectly safe. "The judges will be sitting up on the dunes," she said, "so they'll have a lovely view of the whole beach." Meanwhile, the surf club has quietly moved its rescue boards and flags to the top of the car park.

UPDATE, 4:30 pm: The king tide came in far lower than the weather service forecast. It stopped twenty metres short of the first castle, and Archie's moat stayed completely dry. The weather service says a change in the wind held the water back.

encounters.frame: A letter has arrived from the Hollowgum Astronomy Club.
encounters.text:
Dear Astronomy Club members,

On the night of Friday the 14th, Comet Varga will pass close enough to Earth to be seen without a telescope. It will not return for another 3,000 years, so this really is a once-in-a-lifetime event. The comet will be visible from about 9 pm until midnight, low in the southern sky.

Unfortunately, the weather service is forecasting thick, low cloud over the whole town from late afternoon on the 14th, and it is not expected to clear until Sunday. Low cloud like this usually sits below about 600 metres.

For this reason, the club has booked a bus to the lookout on Mount Ember, which stands 900 metres above sea level. From the summit, members should be looking down on the cloud rather than up at it. The bus leaves the town hall at 6 pm sharp and returns at 1 am. Seats are limited to forty, and thirty-two have already been taken.

Please bring warm clothes, a thermos and a torch with a red cover, because white light ruins everyone's night vision. Members who would rather stay home are welcome to join our online chat, although I'm afraid there may not be much to chat about.

P.S. Late news: the weather service has changed its forecast. The cloud on the 14th will be much thicker than usual, stretching from the ground up to about 1,200 metres.

Clear skies,
Professor Ada Finch, Club President
